cues.text: Chapter three is about KPIs, and the question underneath it is this: how do we know whether a digital transformation is actually succeeding?
Start with the term.
A key performance indicator, or K-P-I, is a measurable indicator tied to a strategic objective.
Notice the two ideas in that definition.
It must be measurable, and it must be tied to a strategic objective.
That is why not every metric is key.
An organisation can measure thousands of things, but a metric becomes a key indicator only when it tells you whether you are moving toward something the strategy says matters.
What makes a KPI useful?
Six qualities.
It is specific, so everyone knows exactly what is being measured.
It is quantifiable, so it can be expressed as a number.
It is goal-oriented, so it connects to an objective.
It is time-bound, so it is judged over a defined period.
It is actionable, so that when the number moves, someone knows what to do about it.
And it is assigned to an owner, a named person or role accountable for it.
A metric with no owner tends to be watched by everyone and acted on by no one.
To make a KPI precise, define six things.
The formula, meaning exactly how it is calculated.
The data source, meaning where the numbers come from.
The baseline, meaning where you are starting.
The target, meaning where you want to get to.
The period, meaning the time window.
And the desired direction, meaning whether a higher or a lower value is better.
That last one matters more than it sounds.
For customer satisfaction, higher is better.
For error rate, lower is better.
If this is not written down, people can read the same chart and disagree about whether it is good news.
Next, a distinction between two kinds of indicators.
Leading indicators signal likely future performance.
The source gives three examples: training competence, adoption of a new workflow, and validated experiments.
If staff are trained and competent, and they are actually using the new workflow, and your experiments have been validated, you have reason to expect good results later.
Lagging indicators measure realised outcomes, results that have already happened.
The examples are retention, revenue and cost reduction.
Think of it like driving.
A leading indicator is the road ahead, and a lagging indicator is the distance you have already covered.
A balanced measurement system combines both.
Leading indicators give you time to react, and lagging indicators confirm whether the result was really achieved.
A balanced system also monitors unintended consequences, meaning side effects you did not plan for, such as a gain in one area that quietly causes harm in another.
Now the table.
It has two columns, Dimension and Measures, and six rows, which show that transformation should be measured from several angles, not just one.
First row, Customer.
The measures are CSAT, which is customer satisfaction score, NPS, which is Net Promoter Score, retention, task completion, and customer effort.
So we look at how happy customers are, how likely they are to recommend us, whether they stay, whether they can complete what they came to do, and how hard they had to work to do it.
Second row, Financial.
Digital revenue, ROI, which is return on investment, cost per transaction, and margin.
These show whether digital activity brings in money, whether investments pay back, how much each transaction costs, and how much is left after costs.
Third row, Operational.
Cycle time, throughput, uptime, and error rate.
That is how long a process takes from start to finish, how much work gets through in a period, how much of the time systems are running, and how often things go wrong.
Fourth row, People.
Engagement, digital skills, adoption, and collaboration.
Transformation depends on people, so we measure whether they are engaged, whether they have the skills, whether they use the new tools, and whether they work well together.
Fifth row, Innovation.
Idea implementation, time to market, and revenue from new products.
These show whether ideas are actually being turned into reality, how fast new offerings reach customers, and whether those offerings earn money.
Sixth row, Agility.
Lead time, cycle time, deployment frequency, and change failure rate.

This is about how quickly and how safely the organisation can change: how long work takes from request to delivery, how long it takes to complete once started, how often changes are released, and what share of those changes fail.
Now the worked examples.
Following the numbers step by step is the best way to make these formulas stick.
First, adoption.
Suppose 360 of 450 eligible employees actively use a new system.
Divide 360 by 450 and you get 0.8, which is 80 percent.
The source adds an important warning: define meaningful active use, not just account creation.
If counting an account as adoption means everyone who was given a login, you could report a high figure while almost nobody is really using the system.
Second, cost per transaction.
Monthly attributable cost is six million naira, and there are 120,000 transactions.
Divide six million by 120,000 and you get fifty naira per transaction.
The word attributable matters.
Only the costs that genuinely belong to that activity should be counted.
Third, availability.
A target of 99.9 percent over 30 days allows about 43.2 minutes of unavailability.
This assumes a time-based measure over 43,200 minutes.
Here is where that comes from.
Thirty days times 24 hours times 60 minutes gives 43,200 minutes.
Availability of 99.9 percent means the system may be unavailable for the remaining 0.1 percent.
Take 0.1 percent of 43,200 and you get 43.2 minutes.
Remember the assumption: this is calculated by time.
A different method, for example one based on counting requests, would give a different answer.
Fourth, ROI.
Benefits are fifteen million naira and costs are ten million naira.
Subtract costs from benefits to get a net gain of five million.
Divide by the cost of ten million, and you get 0.5, or 50 percent.
The source says this is over the stated period, so an ROI figure is always tied to a time frame.
Fifth, NPS.
Sixty percent of respondents are promoters and twenty-five percent are detractors.
Net Promoter Score is promoters minus detractors, so sixty minus twenty-five gives 35.
Notice that it is expressed as a number, not a percentage.
Sixth, relative change, which often confuses people.
If delivery time falls from 20 days to 15 days, that is a drop of five days.
Five divided by twenty is 25 percent, so it is a 25 percent reduction.
Now take a rate that rises from 40 percent to 50 percent.
The simple difference is 10 percentage points.
But relative to the starting value of 40, an increase of 10 is 25 percent.
So the same change can be described as 10 percentage points or as a 25 percent relative increase.
Both are correct, but they are different statements, and a good report says which one it means.
Finally, the traps.
Avoid vanity metrics.
The source's example is downloads without sustained use.
A big download count looks impressive, but if people install an app and never come back, it says little about real value.
Avoid ambiguous denominators.
If it is unclear what you are dividing by, such as all employees or only eligible employees, the percentage can mean very different things.
Avoid cherry-picked periods, where you choose the time window that makes the result look best.
And be aware of Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it can lose usefulness.
Once people are rewarded for hitting the number, they may find ways to improve the number without improving the thing it was meant to represent.
The last point ties the chapter together.
Faster releases with worsening failures are not necessarily success.
If deployment frequency goes up but the change failure rate rises too, the speed is not delivering real value.
This is why we pair measures, combine leading and lagging indicators, and watch for unintended consequences.
